name: Maya religion
info: Traditional Maya religion is the religion of the Maya peoples of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras and southern Mexico, a recognizably distinct tradition for more than two and a half millennia, known for its calendar, offerings and kingly ritual.

facts.origin: the Maya area of Mesoamerica, existing for more than two and a half millennia as a recognizably distinct phenomenon; before Christianity it was spread over many indigenous kingdoms with their own local traditions
facts.founder: none named: it grew within the wider frame of Mesoamerican religion, and its priests, diviners and tellers of tales are among its main sources
facts.scriptures: the Dresden, Madrid and Paris codices and the Grolier Codex, inscriptions and the 'ceramic codex' of pottery scenes; the Popol Vuh, the Ritual of the Bacabs and the Chilam Balam books from the early colonial period; a large oral tradition
facts.followers: the extant Maya peoples of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras and southern Mexico, where the religion coexists with Christianity and the Pan-Maya movement

t: Maya religion is to a large extent a complex of ritual practices, sometimes called costumbre: offerings, prayer, purification and sacrifice, with landmarks such as mountains, caves and cenotes as sacred places.
The 260-day calendar, still used by daykeepers, guides life through the 20 named days and 13 numbers, and the Year Bearers and katuns were worshipped as divine lords.
Its pre-Hispanic form is known from Maya codices, inscriptions and pottery scenes and from Spanish colonial writers, and today it is the product of centuries of symbiosis with Roman Catholicism.
dyk: A drink offered at a pre-Hispanic New Year ritual was to be made of exactly 415 grains of parched maize, and on another occasion exactly 49 grains of maize mixed with copal were to be burnt.
ev: The Late Preclassic period (200 BCE to 200 CE), from which stone inscriptions survive, begins
A mural shows a demonic figure of the underworld whose teeth resemble the stalactites of caves
The Classic period (200 to 900 CE) begins, with kingdoms whose rituals of kingship are central to court life
Noblemen from Classic kingdoms go on pilgrimage to the caves of Naj Tunich and record their visits on its walls
The Postclassic period begins, the time of the three surviving Maya hieroglyphic books
Chichen Itza attracts pilgrims from the surrounding kingdoms to its large cenote, and the Yucatec priesthood is hierarchically organised
Friar Diego de Landa writes the only extensive treatment of pre-Spanish Maya ritual by a near-contemporary
The Tzeltal Rebellion in Chiapas centres on the cult of the Virgin Mary

sections.origins:
Traditional Maya religion is part of the wider frame of Mesoamerican religion. When its pre-Hispanic antecedents are taken into account, it has existed for more than two and a half millennia as a recognizably distinct phenomenon. Before Christianity it was spread over many indigenous kingdoms, each with its own local traditions. No founder is named. Today it is held by the extant Maya peoples of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras and the Mexican states of Tabasco, Chiapas, Quintana Roo, Campeche and Yucatán.

What is known of the pre-Hispanic religion comes from several kinds of source, the primary ones of Maya origin. They include the three surviving Maya hieroglyphic books, the Dresden, Madrid and Paris codices, and the Maya-Toltec Grolier Codex, all from the Postclassic period after 900 CE; the 'ceramic codex' of pottery scenes and texts; mural paintings; and stone inscriptions from the Classic (200 to 900 CE) and Late Preclassic (200 BCE to 200 CE) periods. The Maya peoples themselves, their priests, diviners and tellers of tales, are also valuable sources, as are the anthropologists and historians who have studied them.

Like many other contemporary Mesoamerican religions, it results from centuries of symbiosis with Roman Catholicism. It now coexists and interacts with pan-Mayan syncretism, the 're-invention of tradition' by the Pan-Maya movement, and Christianity in its various denominations.
sections.beliefs:
To a large extent Maya religion is a complex of ritual practices, sometimes called costumbre, the 'custom' set against orthodox Roman Catholic ritual. The Maya landscape is a ritual topography in which mountains, wells and caves are assigned to specific ancestors and deities. Offerings, such as special maize breads, maize and cacao drinks, honey liquor, flowers, incense and cigars, establish and renew relations, called 'contracts' or 'covenants', with the other world, and prayer almost invariably accompanies them. Purification by fasting, sexual abstention, bathing and, especially in the past, confession generally precedes major rituals.

The world is conceived as a square or circular earth with a tree for each direction, a sky of thirteen layers and an underworld often thought to have nine. A tree of life stands at the centre. The principal creator god of the codices is Itzamna, and other deities include Chaac, the rain god, and the maize god. The ancient concept of deity cannot be reduced to a personification of nature: deities have social functions and can be patrons of kin groups and places. Maya believe each person has several souls, and loss of a soul causes illness. Among the Yucatec, evildoers descended to an underworld, the metnal, while others went to a sort of paradise. Pre-Hispanic ideas of the afterlife may never have been unified.
sections.texts:
The Maya codices are books of ritual and divination. The Dresden Codex depicts the New Year rites and, in its astrology, lunar and solar eclipses and the cycles of Venus; the Paris Codex contains what some consider to be a zodiac. The Classic period left stone inscriptions and the pottery scenes of the 'ceramic codex', the most important sources for Classic mythology, though the two narratives recognised so far, about the Hero Twins and the maize god, must be reconstructed from scenes in which narrative and ritual are intertwined.

From the early colonial period come the Popol Vuh, the Ritual of the Bacabs and, at least in part, the Chilam Balam books. The Popol Vuh, written in Quiché, contains the earliest prayers recorded in European script, embedded in its creation myths, and tells the story of the hero twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque and of a succession of earlier mankinds. The Ritual of the Bacabs is the main collection of ancient Yucatec curing rituals. Some Chilam Balam books present a deluge myth and show the colonial Maya's interest in the astrology of their conquerors.

Much knowledge of pre-Hispanic ritual comes through Spanish writers. Diego de Landa's account of Yucatán, written about 1566, is the only extensive treatment by a near-contemporary, though agriculture and kingship are hardly touched in it. Las Casas wrote for the Highland Maya.
sections.spread:
Before the Spanish conquest the religion was spread over many indigenous kingdoms, each with local traditions, and pilgrimage connected places across the Maya area. About 1500 Chichen Itza drew pilgrims from the surrounding kingdoms to its large cenote, and other pilgrims visited shrines such as those of Ix Chel and other goddesses on the islands off Yucatán's east coast. Eight centuries earlier noblemen from Classic kingdoms had gone to the caves of Naj Tunich and recorded their visits on the walls. Kingdoms named in the sources include Palenque, Tikal, Yaxchilan, Copan, Quirigua, Maní, Q'umarkaj and Chichen Itza.

Its later history is one of symbiosis with Roman Catholicism. Today pilgrimages often involve visits of village saints, represented by statues, and farther sanctuaries such as the thirteen sacred mountains visited by the Q'eqchi'. Local forms differ: the Tzotzil of Zinacantan, the K'iche' of Momostenango, the Tz'utujil of Santiago Atitlán, the Ch'orti', the Lacandon and the Yucatec each have their own practice. Since the conquest, Maya societies have known religious 'revitalisation' movements, some of a violent character, responding to exploitation by non-Maya outsiders: the Tzeltal Rebellion of 1712 in Chiapas, the 'Caste War' in eastern Yucatán in the late 19th century, in which a 'Talking Cross' played the main role, and movements in the Alta Verapaz.
sections.community:
Maya religion has its own religious functionaries, often hierarchically organised, who pray and sacrifice on behalf of lineages, local groups or the whole community. In many places they work within the Catholic brotherhoods (cofradías) and the civil-religious hierarchy, or cargo system, which have played a crucial role in preserving pre-Spanish traditions. Yucatec village priests are called jmen ('practitioner'); the Ch'orti' have 'godfathers of the wet season'; communities in the northwestern highlands of Guatemala have 'Prayermakers'; and diviners ('daykeepers') and curers are active nearly everywhere. Feasts are usually organised by religious brotherhoods.

Knowledge of the earlier priesthood rests almost entirely on Spanish missionaries. About 1500 the Yucatec priesthood was hierarchically organised, from a high priest at court down to priests in the towns, with the general word ah k'in, 'calendrical priest'. Special offices included the oracle (chilan), the astrologer and the sacrificer of human beings (nacom). Access to the late Postclassic priesthood seems to have been restricted to the nobility. The Classic king, the k'uhul ajaw or 'holy lord', acted ex officio as a priest, and the rituals of kingship were the most important of the Maya court. Pre-Hispanic sacrifice usually used animals, but on exceptional occasions, such as a ruler's accession, severe illness or burial, or drought and famine, it included human beings, adults and children. Bloodletting by high officials and royal family members was characteristic.
sections.legacy:
The 260-day calendar has proved particularly resistant to time. Today a daykeeper may stand before a fire and pray in Maya to the 260 days, the cardinal directions, the ancestors, towns, lakes, caves or volcanoes, and people consult daykeepers about baby names and wedding dates. The Yucatec Maya continue the Hetz mek ritual, performed about three months after birth, in which a child is offered implements and, if it grasps them, this is considered a foretelling. Contemporary sacrificial rites emphasise the sprinkling of blood, especially that of turkeys, and healing rituals focus on retrieving lost souls.

Catholic and traditional elements have merged: the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, saints, archangels and the devil have usually merged with traditional deities, patron deities and ancestral heroes, and angels generally represent rain deities. The figure of Maximón venerated in Santiago Atitlán is an example. The ethics of Maya religion are hard to compare with those of the monotheistic world religions and cannot be analysed with a contemporary understanding of ethics, though both share the idea of 'covenants' between deities and human beings; the archaic practice of human sacrifice is to be viewed within this framework.

summary: Traditional Maya religion is the ritual religion of the Maya peoples of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras and southern Mexico, distinct for more than two and a half millennia. Known from codices, inscriptions and Spanish writers, it centres on offerings, a 260-day calendar and kingly ritual, and today is the product of centuries of symbiosis with Roman Catholicism.
references: Barbara Tedlock,, Time and the Highland Maya (University of New Mexico Pres, 1992)
J.E.S. Thompson,, Maya History and Religion (University of Oklahoma Press, 1970)
notes: Start -500 circa: the article says only 'more than two and a half millennia as a recognizably distinct phenomenon'; the earliest dated items are Late Preclassic inscriptions (200 BCE to 200 CE) and a mural of about 100 BCE. The map's earliest areas start at -200 for that reason.

Event 'c. 700' is my reading of 'Eight centuries earlier' than c. 1500 (Naj Tunich pilgrimage); the article gives no year. 'c. 1566' is Landa's date as the article gives it. Event 200 and 900 are period boundaries as the article gives them; the Classic period's rituals of kingship are from the article's Kingship section.
Founder: the article names none; I did not call the Popol Vuh or the codices scripture except as sources. The article gives no figure for followers.

Left out: detailed descriptions of the New Year rites, rain-making rituals said to be secretive, black sorcery, the Classic 'star war' and calendrical numerology; the wayob/co-essence and the spook sections beyond a mention.

The 'legacy' section's last sentence puts the article's Ethics paragraph in a hedged form; read it first. The 'spread' section lists kingdoms named in the article (Palenque, Tikal, Yaxchilan, Copan, Quirigua, Maní, Q'umarkaj, Chichen Itza); the article does not call them a spread but 'many indigenous kingdoms'.
The article says Landa wrote 'ca. 1566' and calls Chichen Itza's pilgrim role 'around 1500'; Cogolludo is cited for 16th-century Yucatán but I left him out.
